sessions.name: Network Effects and Defensibility
sessions.description:
Pre-Readings:


  • Seven Questions to Evaluate Network Effect Moats - Platform Chronicles
  • Tactics for Improving Marketplace Quality [Video] - Josh Breinlinger (our guest for today!)


Supplementary Materials﻿:


  • How Defensible are Zoom's Network Effects - Platform Chronicles
  • The Network Effects Manual: 13 Different Network Effects (and counting) - NfX
sessions.summary:
Summary 🧠


  • Securing a well-defined network effects and increasing lock-in is key to success.
  • There are 2 types of network effects: same side (e.g., Zoom and Discord) and cross side (e.g., Amazon and Alibaba).
  • Not all network effects lead to winner-takes-all. You need a network effect with high marginal value, a differentiated supply side, invested suppliers, global reach, high switching costs, high cost of coordination, and synchronous matching.


Important Terminology 


  • Network effects - when a product or service gets more valuable when more customers use it.
  • Same side Network Effects - when the value of a platform increases because the number of users increases (e.g., Zoom and Discord).
  • Cross Side Network Effects - when a platform depends on 2 or more user groups such as buyers and sellers (e.g., Amazon, Alibaba, and Airbnb).



Guest Speaker Josh Breinlinger, CEO of Turtle Venture Insights 💡


When you are looking at factors of a business to evaluate network effects, what would they be?


  1. A massive existing market
  2. Most of the really big success stories in tech are taking an existing market and making it much better (eg., blockbuster to Netflix).
  3. BUT a preexisting condition is that there is a ton of inefficiency in the market that can be improved upon.
  4. Cohort retention
  5. For platforms, you need both buyer retention and seller retention to drive liquidity.
  6. In the marketplace, liquidity is the product and is a MUST HAVE 
  7. That is why Craigslist is successful even though they have a seemingly outdated product


How do you help companies enhance their network effects?

  • Understand the company’s flywheel and each point within the flywheel. Each point should have a KPI associated with it.


What should founders think about when designing and regulating their marketplaces?

  • Ask: What is the “happy path” that people want?
  • E.g., For Thermal Travel, which is a marketplace for packaged travel, the happy path is 1) you go on the website 2) you find the trip 3) you book the trip 4) you have fun on the trip. 
  • Some things disrupt this happy path (e.g., delays, rescheduling, etc.)
  • Your job is to maximize the “happy path” percentage.
  • Don’t just look at feedback!
  • Feedback only shows who is bad, not who is good.
  • Use other signals: 
  • E.g., Show or no show, Repeat purchases, etc.


What is an example of a business with good network effects but failed?

  • MySpace: It had huge network effects initially but a bad user experience along with widespread fraud within the platform allowed Facebook to come in and clean up inefficiencies.
  • VRBO: launched way before Airbnb but the same thing happened with bad user experience and inefficiencies that Airbnb came to clean up.



What are Network Effects? 👭👬👫


  • Network effects occur when a product or service gets more valuable when more customers use it.


There are two types of Network Effects 

  • Same side Network Effects - when the value of a platform increases because the number of users increases (e.g., Zoom and Discord).
  • Cross Side Network Effects - when a platform depends on 2 or more user groups such as buyers and sellers (e.g., Amazon, Alibaba, and Airbnb).
  • Facebook exhibits both same side and cross side network effects: users <-> users, users <-> app developers.


An interesting case of network effects: Craigslist ☮️

  • The amazing thing about Craigslist is they have not updated their website since 1995 but they are still highly relevant today solely due to network effects.
  • Crazy stats: In 2019, they had around $1 billion revenue, 90% margin, with 50 employees.
  • Only the recently-created Facebook marketplace has been able to give Craigslist some decent competition.


Key Point: While network effects can create highly defensible market positions, not all network effects are defensible and lead to “winner-takes-all”



Under what conditions do network effects lead to defensible market positions? 8 questions to help determine this: 🛡🛡🛡


1) How much do users really care about other users adopting the same products/service?

  1. If there are weak network effects, users don’t really care:
  2. E.g., WeWork tenants and their service providers have weak network effects
  3. Users also don’t care if a product/service simply exhibits virality, which is often confused to be network effects.
  4. E.g., GoPro's focus on social sports, which led to skyrocketing sales, does NOT exhibit network effects. This is virality.
  5. Users don’t care if it isn’t the actual product exhibiting network effects, but rather the market itself.
  6. E.g., Fax machines have a network effect but individual brands like Xerox don’t because the network effect is market-level, not product-level.
  7. Lastly, users don’t care if the transaction size is small.
  8. Avoid marketplaces with infrequent/small transactions.


Takeaway: Any product can create virality; few products have real network effects.


2) What is the marginal value of the network effect?

Description: Above are 2 patterns of network effects that both converge to the same end result.


  • If you’re the first mover, which is better? Network Effect #2!
  • Why? The problem with network effects #1 is it is less defensible: any competitor can get close with a pretty small number of users due to the huge surge in the beginning. Towards the end, it begins to plateau.
  • Network effect #2 increases at a constant rate, which is much more defensible because it doesn’t plateau.
  • How do you figure out the “slope” of your network effect? Figure out how fragmented the demand-side or supply-side is
  • More fragmentation (on both the demand and supply side) leads to a higher marginal value of network effects, which is more defensible.
  • Can network effects turn negative at some point? YES
  • E.g., congestion on blockchains and spam/misinformation on social media.


Takeaway: You want network effects with high marginal value, which can be achieved with more fragmentation on both the demand side and the supply side.


3) Commodity vs. differentiated supplier? 👩‍🎤🧑‍🎤👨‍🎤

  • Differentiated is much better for network effects
  • E.g., Cameo allows users to pay for personalized messages/videos from celebrities, which are differentiated suppliers. Hopps provides companies with experts for digital commerce & marketing, which are commodity suppliers.


Takeaway: You want differentiated suppliers because it would be harder for competitors to come in and imitate you.


4) How invested are suppliers in the platform?

  • Most successful 2-sided marketplaces rely on heavily invested suppliers.
  • E.g., Power sellers on eBay and super hosts on Airbnb.


Takeaway: You want heavily invested suppliers to drive smoother and better transactions.


5) Which is better: global or local network effects?

  • Global is much better
  • E.g., Uber is more of a local network, which doesn't have network effects as strong as Airbnb, which is global. 
  • It is much harder for Uber to leverage its network effects when it goes to different locations. 
  • This is why it has lost to so many global competitors (e.g., Didi)

﻿

6) Switching and multihoming costs?

  • Low switching/multihoming costs lead to lower defensibility.
  • E.g., it’s so easy for riders and drivers to switch between Uber and Lyft that even if there is a network effect, there is no defensibility behind that network effect.
  • How can you drive up switching costs?
  • Non-monetary incentives are preferred (e.g., preferential algorithmic treatment for drivers/riders with more rides on the platform).
  • Monetary incentives (e.g., discounts and monthly passes) are typically ineffective and sustainable.


Takeaway: You want high switching costs, and to do this, you need to use non-monetary incentives to make users stay on your platform.


7) Ease of coordination among users? 

  • In some cases, users already know their interaction/transaction partners and can easily coordinate which platform to use.
  • E.g., Video chat apps like Skype and Whatsapp
  • While ease of coordination can help overcome the initial chicken and egg problem, this leads to low defensibility as users can easily coordinate with one another to use another platform (low switching costs).


Takeaway: You want to increase the cost of coordination by enabling the discovery of new interactions of transaction partners.


8) Synchronous vs asynchronous matching?

  • Uber is synchronous - if I want to order a ride, it comes to me immediately.
  • BlaBlaCar is asynchronous - if I want to order a long-distance car ride, it could come tomorrow.


Takeaway: Although Synchronous matching requires more liquidity and results in a harder chicken and egg problem, it is preferred because it is more defensible.

sessions.name: Data Network Effects
sessions.description:
Pre-Readings:


  • When Data Creates Competitive Advantage - Harvard Business Review
  • The VC View of Platforms [Video] - Simon Rothman (our guest for today!)


Supplementary Materials:


  • Uber, the Startup Steroid Era and the Use of Capital as a Performance-Enhancing Drug - Simon Rothman
  • Why Are Data Network Effects Less Valuable Than Regular Network Effects? - Platform Chronicles
  • Six Questions To Evaluate Data-enabled Learning Moats - Platform Chronicles
  • 19 Tactics to Solve the Chicken-or-Egg Problem and Grow Your Marketplace - NfX
sessions.summary:
Summary 🧠


  • Data-enabled learning allows firms to improve their products by leveraging customer data.
  • There are 3 types of DEL: across user, same user, and a combo of both.
  • DEL only really creates network effects if:
  1. Value added is higher than standalone value.
  2. The marginal value of DEL doesn’t diminish.
  3. Relevance of user data depreciates slowly.
  4. It’s hard to obtain alternative sources of data.
  5. It’s hard to imitate data-driven product improvements.
  6. Data leads to across user and same user product improvement.
  7. You have a head start in your data and algorithm.
  • While DEL will become “table stakes,” it doesn’t guarantee defensibly competitive positions or network effects.
  • The most valuable/powerful businesses will be built on both data network effects and regular network effects


Important Terminology 


  • Data-Enabled Learning (DEL) - firms can improve their products via more customer data.
  • Learning across users - as a product gains more users/data, it improves the product (e.g., Grammarly)
  • Learning from user’s repeated usage - value goes up for a single user as they use it more (e.g., Nest Thermostat, Eight Sleep bed)
  • Combo of both - recommender systems use others’ data and your personalized data to drive defensibility and network effects (e.g., Netflix, Spotify, and TikTok).



Insights from Guest Speaker Simon Rothman of Greylock💡


What key factors do you look at when observing marketplaces?

  1. Supply and demand have to have a minimum efficient scale.
  2. Supply should have enough assortment for sufficient demand in the future
  3. E.g., Uber should have enough vehicles so they can have a pickup SLA that is reasonable.
  4. Metrics that show how close a company is to PMF.
  5. Conversion rate:
  6. What is the probability that the product will sell?
  7. What is the probability that the service provider will get a living wage?
  8. Retention rate/usage rate of each cohort:
  9. This is a great metric because it’s hard to cheat whether a customer actually likes you if their actions are identifiable. 
  10. Better marketplaces have higher retention.


Do you also look at broader things about the potential of a marketplace?

  1. Is the company more like a digital broker than an actual marketplace?
  2. Companies that do a lot of the manual work (e.g., phone calls) during the matchmaking process rather than naturally let the buyer and seller match on their platform are more like digital brokers than marketplaces.
  3. In a marketplace, buyers and sellers should naturally match with each other on the platform without interference.
  4. Does the company rely on long-term assets on the balance sheet?
  5. If so, it is not really a marketplace.
  6. Marketplaces are an intermediary; they simply are a platform for matching a buyer and a seller.
  7. It’s fine if a company relies on short-term assets to kickstart their marketplace, but it shouldn’t be their sustainable advantage.


Are there metrics you look at to measure defensibility?

  • Not really. Usually, if strong network effects are in place (post-PMF), a business is already very defensive.
  • The problem is before this happens, a business is very vulnerable, and many founders incorrectly believe that they are defensive at this point.


Can you talk about the difference between B2B marketplaces and consumer marketplaces?

  • Consumers are very flexible and fluid. Enterprises are not.
  • Therefore, B2B is less flexible and has a lot more friction due to exclusivity, contracts, etc.
  • B2B growth is very chunky due to contracts with large enterprises. Consumer growth is smooth as gradual increases in demand come from small individual customers.
  • While this can lead to faster growth, the “chunkiness” makes B2B more vulnerable because the marketplace initially has no leverage over its customer.
  • B2Bs can only build leverage when they gain enough demand from other enterprise customers.
  • For consumer marketplaces, you are more valuable and have greater leverage from day 1.


What about C2C?

  • C2C is the hardest to build but the most defensible.
  • If a C2C platform is liquid, the take rate is higher because consumer sellers and buyers have less leverage over the platform.
  • For most defensible, you would lean toward C2C because the network has all the power.
  • E.g., Craigslist and eBay


﻿


1) What is data enabled learning (DEL)? 📊📈📉


  • DEL - firms can improve their products via more customer data.
  • More customers -> More data -> Better product

Different types of DEL

  • Learning across users - as a product gains more users/data, it improves the product (e.g., Grammarly)
  • This is necessary for data network effects
  • Learning from user’s repeated usage - value goes up for a single user as they use it more (e.g., Nest Thermostat, Eight Sleep bed)
  • This leads to increasing switching costs, which increases defensibility but doesn’t drive network effects.
  • Combo of both - recommender systems use others’ data and your personalized data to drive defensibility and network effects (e.g., Netflix, Spotify, and TikTok).

What has changed to make data so important?

  1. Digitization and cloud based products/services.
  2. Cheaper storage and better data processing (AI/ML).
  • Implications of these changes:
  • Increased speed and scope of gathering customer data
  • Companies can improve quality while products are still being consumed.
  • Learning from customer data can be a key factor in determining the quality of products.
  • The learning is personalized to each product user.

Key Point: The scope for data network effects have become much larger.


2) Under what conditions does DEL really create network effects and competitive advantage? 📊📈📉 ➡ 👭👬👫


1. What is the value added by customer data relative to stand-alone value?

  • The value added by DEL could vary widely depending on your product
  • E.g., Smart TV vs. Autonomous vehicles
  • Smart TVs: value added with DEL through recommender systems is low.
  • Customers won’t be thinking about how good the recommender system is when buying the TV. They look at other factors (e.g., screen quality).
  • For autonomous vehicles, value added through DEL is paramount as it directly relates to the performance and safety of the vehicle.

Takeaway: DEL will only lead to network effects if the value added by customer data is significantly larger than the standalone value.


2. What is the marginal value of data enabled learning?

  • Nest vs. Credit score
  • Nest: Exhibits product #2 because data collection and learning is quick and easy. As people use the product more, this leads to larger data collection, and the value of the product gets progressively higher and higher.
  • Credit Score: Exhibits product #1 because it’s much harder, more expensive, and more time-consuming to collect data for defaults, which are rare.

Takeaway: DEL only leads to network effects if its marginal value doesn’t diminish and continues to push the value of the product higher and higher.


3. How fast does the relevance of the user data depreciate?

  • E.g., Google Maps vs. SeeTrue
  • Google maps: Data depreciates quickly because it isn’t very useful after you get to your destination.
  • SeeTrue (trains airport security to detect threats): data depreciation is slow because past data is going to be used for future learning to detect new threats.

Takeaway: You want slowly depreciating data so it will be hard for emerging companies to catch up to your data advantage/learning.


4. How difficult is it to acquire alternative sources of data?

  • E.g., X.ai vs Zero Spam
  • Zero Spam (a spam filter): it’s easy to collect email data with spam in it, so it’s also easy for other companies to acquire this data.
  • X.ai (allows you to set up meetings on your calendar via a virtual assistant): It’s extremely difficult to collect data on a person chatting with a virtual assistant.

Takeaway: If it is easy to acquire alternative sources of data, it won’t be defensible because other companies can also easily acquire that data.


5. How hard is it to imitate data-driven product improvements?

  • My Starbucks Idea vs. XM Voice Analytics:
  • My Starbucks Idea: A ranking system shows the most popular requests on the website, making it easy to imitate the data-driven product improvements.
  • XM Voice Analytics: The data is engineered on users’ voices and shows improvements and outcomes, but learning is hidden. Therefore, the results are hard to reverse-engineer.

Takeaway: You want your data-enabled product improvements to be hidden and hard to imitate.


6. Does data from one user improve the product for the same user, other users, or both?

  • E.g., Eight Sleep Bed vs. autonomous tractors
  • Eight Sleep Bed: Data from one user only improves the product for the same user because one person’s sleep pattern is much different from others.
  • Autonomous tractors: 
  • Data from one tractor improves the product for the same tractor by allowing it to adapt to the specific environment of the farm. 
  • Data from one tractor also improves the ability for all tractors to initially adapt to their respective environment.

Takeaway: If the data leads to both across user and same user product improvement, it leads to greater network effects.


7. Do you have a head-start in your data and/or your algorithm?

  • If you are facing a market where there are incumbents with a great data advantage, you are at a huge disadvantage
  • E.g., It’s hard for Bing to catch up to Google because of its data advantage, which results in better search results.

Takeaway: You want a head start in your data and algorithm.


3) Data Network Effects vs. Regular Network Effects


Key differences between the two

  • The cold start problem is often not as hard with data (usually you can buy data to start off).
  • Data network effects often run out of steam sooner
  • With normal network effects, you may have millions of users before network effects start diminishing
  • Data learning may quickly depreciate
  • The coordination problem is less likely to arise for new users.
  • People are less likely to think about what other users are choosing because it isn’t as obvious to them

Poll: Does google search enjoy defensibility because of same side data network effects?

  • YES! The data creates the network effect and the defensibility comes from the coordination problem. The more you use it, the better Google becomes for you. If Google wasn’t able to learn from data, there would be no point for you to stay on the platform.

sessions.name: Transforming Products into Platforms (Part I)
sessions.description:
Pre Readings:


  • Finding the Platform in Your Product - Harvard Business Review
  • PDF Here
  • Growing an app ecosystem [Video] - Kevin Fitzgerald (our guest for today!)
  • The Chicken & Egg Problem - Platform Chronicles [PREVIEW]


Supplementary Materials:


  • Product-to-Platforms (Part I) - Platform Chronicles
  • Product-to-Platforms (Part II) - Platform Chronicles
  • Product-to-Platforms (Part III) - Platform Chronicles
sessions.summary:
Summary 🧠


  • Network effects are a double-edged sword. Without users, you can’t attract suppliers (or other users), and vice versa. This is known as the chicken-and-egg problem.
  • There are 4 approaches to solve the chicken and egg problem: offer a lot of value to one side (single-side mode), bring your own demand, fake one side, or change people’s expectations.
  • Transforming a product into a platform will generate network effects, which results in better defensibility and faster growth.
  • There are three main ways to transform your product: opening the door to 3rd parties (today’s focus), connecting existing customers, and reaching out to customers’ customers.


Important Terminology 


  • Chicken and egg problem: The problem of getting enough critical mass to trigger a positive feedback loop.
  • Single-side mode: Offer enough value to one side so that they will join regardless of what’s on the other side.



Insights from Guest Speaker Kevin Fitzgerald, Managing Director of Xero in Asia 💡


1. What is Xero?

  • A cloud accounting platform that brings powerful technology solutions to SMBs.


2. When does it make sense to transform from product to platform?

  • As early as possible. Doing this not only helps you build a community/ecosystem, but it helps you be deliberate about what product you want to build and how that product evolves into a platform.


3. How big is Xero’s ecosystem?

  • Over 1000 specialists in consolidation, point of sale, inventory management, etc.


4. Has Xero ever had issues with third party providers?

  • Yes. Xero was looking for a tax partner that could build an API-led solution for the various countries it served. 
  • While they found a partner to build tax solutions for SMBs in Indonesia, the partner was more focused on their manufacturing business and viewed their partnership with Xero as a side opportunity.
  • Ultimately, the partnership fell apart.
  • It is crucial to find third-party providers that are dedicated to their commitment.


6. Many 3P SMB products integrate with both Xero and QuickBooks. What are your thoughts on the importance of fostering differentiators (apps that aren't on QuickBooks platform or work better with Xero than with QuickBooks) and strategies for doing so? Or does it matter at all?

  • In many ways, it doesn’t matter because the churn rate is so low (there’s a small chance that customers will abandon Xero to only use Quickbooks).
  • It is more important to show that you are an open platform and that you place customer value as your top priority.


7. Who should be responsible for transforming product to platform

  • At Xero, there’s a dedicated ecosystem team and the head of ecosystem that sets the strategy for building out the ecosystem and setting up the transformation from product to platform.


8. How do you address the difficulties in finding a third party? How do you screen for fit?

  • In the early years, business developers would be sent directly to regions of interest to identify solutions that are needed and source third parties.
  • Third parties get passed through the ecosystem development team for review, where the team will score the partner after running them through various tests.


10. How do you monetize your ecosystem?

  • Xero was more focused on building a healthy ecosystem rather than building an additional revenue stream.
  • This is especially important considering Xero serves SMBs, which they don’t want to impose higher costs on.
  • As a result, they have only just begun to implement plans to monetize.



1) Chicken and egg problem: how to start network effects out of thin air? 🐔🥚


What is it? 

  • Chicken and egg problem: The problem of getting enough critical mass to trigger a positive feedback loop.
  • It occurs because network effects are a double-edged sword:
  • How do we grow users without supply?
  • How do we attract supply without users?


4 Approaches to crack it 🐣

  1. Single-side mode: Offer enough value to one side so that they will join regardless of what’s on the other side.
  2. E.g., 
  3. PayPal paid $15 to users for their first $30 spent
  4. Uber employs/hires drivers.
  5. Hipcamp offers free services for searching and booking campsites.
  6. OpenTable offered its software to restaurants at a bargain price to build supply.
  7. Bring your own demand: Get suppliers/creators to bring their existing customers (e.g., Clubhouse’s network effects were driven by their speakers bringing on their fan base to the platform).
  8. Suppliers will bring their existing customers if the platform brings additional value that hasn’t existed prior.
  9. The network effects kick in when customers start exploring other suppliers on the platform.
  10. Fake one side: Make users think that there are a lot of users on one side.
  11. Manually fill the supply 
  12. Use bots (e.g., OfferUp)
  13. Change people’s expectations: Make users expect there will be a lot of users on the other side
  14. Attract a “whale” on one side (e.g., anchor tenants at malls)
  15. Issue white paper and tokens.


Some general principles to follow when trying to crack this problem

  1. Don’t try to charge both sides initially. 
  2. Initially, you want to make the value proposition compelling to only one side.
  3. Which one do you start with? Usually the supply side
  4. There are fewer suppliers in number, and more are willing to try new things to get extra demand
  5. Exceptions: Amazon and Hipcamp
  6. Focus on a narrow segment/vertical first
  7. Narrow geographically, in terms of the product, in terms of time, etc. (e.g., Rover started dog sitting in Seattle, but over time became a global company).
  8. There are exceptions (e.g., OpenSea was less narrowly focused because they didn’t know what type of NFT was going to be the killer product.)
  9. Use a zig-zag strategy
  10. Once you attract a few suppliers, focus on growing demand. Once you’ve built up more demand, go back to growing supply.


Key point: These are the general guiding principles, but there is no “magic” strategy. There is usually a lot of trial-and-error involved.



2) Transforming products into platforms: how to generate network effects around existing products/services? 📱➡


Why do companies want to transform their products into a platform?

  • Fear and Greed: it will generate network effects, which results in better defensibility and faster growth.
  • Not all products should become platforms.


What do we mean by product to platform? Common misconceptions:

  1. The platform shouldn’t be created from scratch. 
  2. It should be tied to an existing product/service.
  3. It doesn’t just involve digital transformations. 
  4. This is the first step for most companies, but it is not, by itself, enough.
  5. These aren’t just “internal” platforms. 
  6. The platform should bring in third parties not controlled by the company.


How can you transform products into platforms? 3 ways

  1. Open the door to 3rd parties to sell their product within your product
  2. E.g., Apple eventually allowed third-party developers to develop apps for their products through the App Store.
  3. E.g., NY sports clubs began opening their space for third parties to host their specialized classes.
  4. Connect existing customers (same product or different products).
  5. Reach out to customers’ customers.


There are several levels involved in opening the door to third parties ➡🚪

  1. Simple advertising of third parties (simplest)
  2. Offer integration with third-party products (e.g., software)
  3. Be a marketplace where third-party products/services are discovered and purchased
  4. Marketplace and integrations (hardest).


Common questions that arise when talking about third-party integration

  • How is this different from outsourcing?
  • When you open up to third parties, your product enables third parties to interact directly with your customers.
  • What if your third parties are competitors?
  • It is very important NOT to exclude competitors
  • Make your higher-quality competitor into a complementor UNLESS that third party competes with the core of your product
  • E.g., Epic trying to create their own operating system for games and selling it on the App Store competes with the core of the App Store.


Tradeoffs of opening the door to third parties

  • Pros:
  • Increases the demand for your product and increases the stickiness of the core product.
  • New revenue streams
  • Allows you to learn from 3rd party sales
  • Cons
  • Integration costs
  • Even though you don’t have full control over the third party, you are held responsible for bad experiences created by them.
  • Third parties could be partial competitors and you may be promoting them.


Other examples of product to platform

  • Steam: Started off selling only Valve's games, but then opened up to sell games from other developers.
  • Alo: Yoga clothes brand that acquired a marketplace that allowed them to use Alo Yoga ambassadors (yoga teachers) to create content on the platform for the Alo Yoga customers.
  • Canva: An online graphic design tool enabling everyone to create beautiful designs. It introduced three different marketplaces over time, pivoting from product to platform: a marketplace for design templates, marketplace for design graphics, and marketplace for in-editor apps

sessions.name: Transforming Products into Platforms (Part II)
sessions.description:
Pre Readings:


  • Product-to-Platform (Part IV); Which Products Have Platform Potential - Platform Chronicles


Supplementary Materials:


  • Product-to-Platform (Part V); Substack - Platform Chronicles
  • Product-to-Platform (Part VI); WeWork - Platform Chronicles
sessions.summary:
Summary 🧠


  • There are 2 additional ways to transform products into platforms: connecting existing customers and reaching out to customers’ customers.
  • You can connect existing customers with the same product (e.g., Disney+ GroupWatch) or with a different product (e.g., OpenTable reservation platform).
  • By restricting your platform to product users (rather than opening it up to everyone), stronger network effects will be generated around a more original product.
  • While connecting existing customers could increase stickiness and create new revenue streams, it could also undermine the value of the original product.
  • While there are benefits to reaching out to customers customers’, it could also lead to increased friction with business customers by potentially commoditizing them.



1a) Connect existing customers with the same product


The Idea Behind It 💡



  • There could be some kind of transaction that a product/service can enable that can enhance the value of that product/service.
  • E.g., Disney+ Groupwatch, Steezy online dance classes, and Intuit Quickbooks matching-making feature. 


An Interesting Example: Matchmaking on Intuit Quickbooks 



  • Intuit has 2 types of customers: accountants and SMBs.
  • The matchmaking feature allows Quickbooks’ SMB customers to find accountants among Quickbooks’s other customers.
  • This is similar to a dating app where each SMB and accountant has a profile on the matchmaking platform.


Poll 🗳 Should QuickBooks allow anyone access to the QuickBooks matchmaking feature?

  • No! While opening it to all creates more virality, it doesn’t generate true network effects (e.g., GoPro grew due to virality, not network effects).
  • Exception: early-stage companies should focus on opening up their platform to create virality.


Key Point: By restricting the matchmaking feature to only Intuit users, stronger network effects will be generated around a more original product.


But not all attempts at customer matchmaking are successful ❌🤝

  • E.g., Virgin America “inflight flirting system” 
  • Allowed individuals in different seats to order food and drinks for one another
  • Virgin stopped doing this due to widespread harassment claims, which reveals a downside of connecting existing customers.
  • E.g., Samsung refrigerator dating website
  • Samsung sells refrigerators, so they decided to create a dating site where people matched based on the contents of their refrigerator.


Another Interesting Example: Lego Bricklink 🧱



  • Lego sells kids toys made of various bricks and parts. Bricklink (acquired by Lego) allows for the trading of second-hand parts and sets.
  • Does this risk cannibalizing demand for new parts and sets (which are the main revenue drivers)?
  • Kind of, but Bricklink was already huge before Lego acquired it, so it was logical for Lego to reduce the threat by integrating Bricklink with their typical offerings.



1b) Connecting existing customers with different products 


  • Only applies to companies that sell 2 or more products.


Example 1: Equifax



  • Equifax (credit scoring) has 2 lines of business:
  • Lender side (main side): Providing credit reports and verification
  • Consumer side: Credit score and ID protection
  • They considered creating a digital credit ID (info verified by third parties that is relevant to lending) that allows more instant credit verification between consumers and lenders.
  • This would essentially make them a two-sided platform rather than a firm with 2 products.


Example 2: 23andMe



  • 23andMe’s (genetic testing) has 2 lines of business:
  • Consumer side: Genome testing, ancestry, and health information
  • Biotech/Pharma side: Aggregate genetic data and non-identifiables (e.g., age, gender, environmental info)
  • With personalized testing data, 23andMe could help create personalized medicine for consumers.
  • They could also allow consumers to opt into double-blinded clinical trials to help the biotech/pharma side collect useful information.


Trade-Offs of Connecting Existing Customers 👍👎

  • Benefits
  1. Increase demand for and stickiness of core product
  2. New potential revenue stream
  • Costs
  1. Cost of creating/acquiring the marketplace (e.g., Lego acquiring Bricklink)
  2. Potentially undermining or cannibalizing standalone value of the product (e.g., Bricklink could undermine Lego’s new offerings)
  3. Responsibility for bad experiences on the marketplace (e.g., Virgin in-flight flirting system).



2) Reach out to customers’ customers


The Idea Behind It 💡



  • Sell a complementary product/service to your customers’ customers that is related to the product/service you are selling to your main customers.
  • This only applies to B2B platforms


E.g., Opentable



  • Initially, a B2B that only sold software to restaurants
  • Eventually built a reservation platform for diners.


E.g., Shopify



  • Initially sold backend services to 1m+ active e-commerce stores.
  • Later created shop.app, which allows delivery and payment, but no comparison shopping and limited discovery of other stores. Why?


Shopify doesn’t want to become Amazon because they don’t want to commoditize their e-commerce customers, who will go to another service if they do.


Trade-Offs of Reaching Out to Customers’ Customers 👍👎

  • Pros
  • Enhanced competitive position
  • Increased stickiness of business customers
  • New potential revenue stream
  • Cons
  • Cost of creating the new platform
  • Frictions with business customers from potentially cannibalizing their sales by commoditizing them (e.g., Shopify and Amazon).



How can you tell if your product/service has platform potential?


1. You have a large customer base

  • Products typically have platform potential post-PMF.


2. You can open the door to 3rd parties by:

  1. Fulfilling The 80-20 rule: You provide 80% of the features that merchants need and third-party developers supply the rest.
  2. Bringing 3rd-party pirates to fill in gaps and innovate (e.g., iPhone, AWS, Roblox)
  3. Providing a unique and convenient channel (e.g., convenience stores in Japan)


3. You can connect customers by:

  1. Having scope to exchange tips and best practices (e.g., Tesla, Mathematica user forums).
  2. Providing complementary services (e.g., QuickBooks find-an-accountant).
  3. Enabling secondary market trading (e.g., AngelList).


4. You can reach out to customers’ customers by:

  1. Improving customers’ transactions with their existing customers (e.g., Shopify’s Shop.app)
  2. Helping customers find new customers (e.g., OpenTable).


Substack checks all the marks for turning their product into a platform

  1. They can open the door to third parties.
  2. E.g., writing assistants, copy editors, illustrators, marketers, etc.
  3. Services must be highly specific to writing, distributing, and monetizing newsletters (e.g., NFTs for newsletters, sponsored content).
  4. They can connect existing customers.
  5. Writer forum for exchanging best practices.
  6. Enabling writers to refer readers, cross-sell or co-syndicate content.
  7. They can reach out to customers’ customers.
  8. Already some content discovery and management (e.g., Substack reader)
  9. Reader login and profile -> recommendations and/or bundled subscriptions
  10. The only concern here is if they can remain different from Medium.com, so their customer base won’t be commoditized (e.g., Shopify and Amazon) and leave.

sessions.name: Network Effects Aren't Enough
sessions.description:
Pre Readings:


  • Platform Leakage I - Platform Chronicles
  • The Problems with 5 Star Rating Systems and How to Fix Them - Harvard Business Review
  • Why We Founded Gable - Liza Mash Levin (our guest speaker for today!)


Supplementary Materials:


  • Platform Leakage II - Platform Chronicles
  • Marketplace or Reseller? - Platform Chronicles
  • Moving from Marketplace to Reseller to Optimize the Seller Experience (ThredUp) - Platform Chronicles
  • Network Effects Aren't Enough - Harvard Business Review
  • Do You Really Want to Be and eBay - Harvard Business Review
sessions.summary:
Summary 🧠


  • Leakage occurs when participants meet on the platform but take their transactions off the platform to avoid paying the platform its cut. 
  • The potential for leakage is larger depending on the type of platform. The leakage problem tends to affect:
  1. Platforms that primarily offer discovery and take a high transaction fee.
  2. Platforms with many large transactions.
  3. Platforms with more repeat transactions.
  4. Platforms with more in-person transactions.
  5. Platforms where communication prior to the transaction is common.
  • You can resolve the leakage problem by changing your business model (e.g., setting appropriate fees) or incentivizing sellers/buyers to stay on the platform.
  • The amount of control you have over your platform depends on whether you are a marketplace (low control), a reseller (high control), or a service provider (high control).
  • The higher your control, the higher your cost structure and perceived responsibility.


Important Terminology


  • Leakage - When participants meet on the platform but take their transactions off the platform to avoid paying the platform its cut. 



Insights from Guest Speaker Liza Levin, CEO and Founder of Gable💡


What is Gable?

  • Gable is a workplace-as-a-service platform that seeks to allow remote workers the flexibility to work where they want to and provide companies the tools they need to manage remote workers.


How did you solve the chicken and egg problem?

  • They focused first on growing the supply (the network of locations)
  • They targeted clusters of locations, which drove demand to those locations
  • Network effects were spurred with the addition of new hosts to the platform
  • After they achieved ample supply, they started growing demand


How did you grow locations?

  • Started locally (the bay area) and achieved around 25 locations before actively reaching out to companies.
  • These companies would have a presence in other areas and so Gable would grow the supply in those locations.
  • This process would go on and on.


How do you prevent leakage on your platform?

  • Increasing stickiness on the demand side (enterprise customers).
  • Gable makes sure enterprise customers stay on the platform by solving a huge pain point for them: helping companies set up locations for remote/hybrid work on a recurring basis.
  • Gable provides software to enterprise customers for visibility/data. If they leave the platform, they won’t have access to this software.
  • Optimizing the supply side (the locations themselves).
  • Ensuring location consistency and quality is crucial to preventing leakage.
  1. Most locations already have demand, so Gable doesn’t need to go through the trouble of onboarding.
  • By ensuring a good customer experience, it builds Gable’s credibility/reputation, which increases the likelihood of existing enterprise customers recommending it to their connections.


There are a lot of other startups in this space. What is Gable’s advantage?

  • Gable started pre-covid, where this space really started to become popular.
  • Gable’s business model and software create stickiness for users.
  • Exclusive partnerships


Q&A 🙋🏻‍♀️


When you talk about a new location you are opening, what is your approach?

  • Active sales and references - Gable is more like a B2B company where it sells its software to enterprises.


Other things that you worry about with less control?

  • Minimum requirements that all hosts have to comply with (e.g., wifi)
  • It is critical for Gable to have quality over quantity because the goal is for customers to be repeating.


At some point, bad experiences are bound to happen. How do you deal with that?

  • Very high level of customer success through 24/7 support.
  • Insurance


What are the most important metrics/KPIs?

  • User signup - individuals or companies
  • Stickiness (retention rate after x weeks) - after a certain number of weeks, the customer is considered a “repeat customer.”
  • Upsell - weekly and monthly usage and adoption rate.
  • Satisfaction rate - helps with determining recurring customers.


How do you work out pricing?

  • Gable is not yet at the stage where it can set its own prices because it does not have enough market power, so their customers set the price and Gable simply pushes them in the right direction.
  1. Offer pricing suggestions to the host based on their location and their price sensitivity.
  2. Gable takes a 20% fee in return.
  • This pricing model is similar to Airbnb, which simply provides sellers with suggestions on pricing.



1) How to deal with the leakage problem


What is leakage

  • Leakage happens when participants meet on the platform but take their transactions off the platform to avoid paying the platform its cut. 


The potential for leakage is much larger in some platforms than in others.



1) Extent of discovery vs value-added transaction services

  • Platforms that primarily offer discovery and it’s taking a high transaction fee are more likely to experience leakage problems (e.g., Capterra and Ziprecruiter). 
  • If your platform is primarily adding value to the transaction, the problem of leakage is much less of a concern (e.g., PayPal).


2) Extent to which the “ideal” business model is (large) per transaction fee.

  • If transactions are small, there is little incentive to go outside the platform to make that transaction.
  • E.g., Airbnb vs. Redbubble


3) Extent to which parties are in a repeated relationship

  • E.g., For CoachUp, you meet your coach repeatedly (more incentive to leak) vs Uber, you meet your driver once (less incentive to go off the platform).


4) Extent to which parties meet in person

  • Transactions that occur in person tend to result in greater amounts of leakage.
  • E.g., CoachUp (you meet your coach in person) vs. Playbook/Fiverr (two parties transact online).


5) Extent to which parties need to communicate prior to a transaction

  • Thumbtack (more leakage because you communicate a lot before the transaction) vs. Uber (less leakage because you only interact after you book the ride).


Solving the leakage problem by setting the appropriate business model 


1) Set appropriate fees

  • Use percentage fees rather than a fixed dollar amount.
  • Dollar (fixed) amount leads to a lot of smaller transactions occurring outside the marketplace
  • Don’t charge high percentage fees
  • Charge more for new clients than old clients
  • You may need to rely on other types of fees
  • Subcription/listing fees (e.g., Thumbtack)
  • Referral fees (e.g., Caterra)
  • Fees to be promoted (e.g., Taobao didn’t have a take rate but rather charged sellers for being at the top of the site)
  • May even need to rely on advertising revenues if you can’t charge the sellers/buyers directly (e.g., Youtube).


2) Hire suppliers directly (e.g., McKinsey & Co hires their own consultants vs. GLG)

  • In this case, you are not a marketplace anymore, but a service provider.


Solving the leakage problem through incentives (carrots and sticks) 🥕


1) Maximize the value of staying on the platform (carrots)

  • E.g., Amazon, Airbnb, and AngelList
  • Standardize your contracts
  • Manage dynamic schedules for service providers
  • Keep transaction records and provide analytics for suppliers
  • Provide sellers dispute resolution
  • Build reputation; promote the seller if they transaction through the platform


2) Hide the identity of users or attempts to steer users to another platform (stick)

  • Users can’t see identities
  • Exchange of identity information is blocked
  • Caveat: this can annoy suppliers


3) Use rankings and reviews (sticks)

  • If you find suppliers taking customers off the platform, rank them lower on the platform
  • E.g., Hotels on Expedia that does their transactions outside of Expedia will get a lower ranking.
  • Design a review system that value reviews from existing repeat customers


4) Ban activities that lead to leakage (sticks)

  • Kick out sellers that undercut the price outside the platform
  • Price parity clauses
  • Problems with this method:
  • This requires significant monitoring
  • May be considered anticompetitive
  • Sellers can find subtle ways to encourage leakage.


Concluding thoughts on leakage

  • Address leakage before embarking on aggressive growth
  • Otherwise, you will burn through money, but have a retention problem
  • Leakage may be masked in early-stage marketplaces because most business is from new customers rather than repeat customers


2) How much control to take 💪💪


The amount of control you have depends on whether you are a marketplace or a reseller/service provider.



  • For marketplaces, it’s harder to take control because sellers set the price.
  • It’s easier for resellers to take control because they set the price (e.g., Zappos).
  • It’s also easier for service providers to take control because they hire their own supply (e.g., McKinsey & Co.)


Cost Structure vs. Control



  • The greater control you have, the higher your cost structure.
  • With less control, you have a lower cost structure
  • To have high control but a low cost structure is impossible


When you want to have more control


  • When you have an information advantage (e.g., Uber drivers have no market information to set prices efficiently so Uber does that for them. eBay sellers have plenty of information on pricing)
  • When user experience is crucial (e.g., Zappos/Steezy for buyers)
  • When a long tail isn’t important (e.g., Amazon with batteries vs Etsy)
  • If you want cross-product spillovers (e.g., Netflix vs Airbnb)
  • To deal with the chicken and egg problem (e.g., Amazon in 1995 vs Amazon in 2021)
  • If you are held responsible for bad outcomes (GLG vs. Craigslist).


Control vs. Responsibility for Platforms



  • If you don’t take a lot of control, no one assigns you responsibility (e.g., Craigslist).
  • If you have some level of control, perceived responsibility increases dramatically.
